subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.activity_title: First Encounter — Read-Aloud and Shared Reading

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites students to look at the title 'Gone with the Scooter' and predict aloud what the story might be about. One or two predictions are noted on the board without judgment.

Teacher reads the story (pp. 11–15) aloud expressively, pausing briefly at key moments — Gopi's search through the garden, the playground exchange, and the comic ending — so students can absorb the events and dialogue.
Shared reading: the class reads the story again together, with different students reading a paragraph each. The teacher models phrasing and expression when students stumble.
Brief whole-class discussion: students share one thing that surprised them and one thing they found funny. No written response is required at this stage.

periods.teacher_notes: This sitting gives students their first full experience of the story through a teacher read-aloud followed by shared reading. The comic ending — the ball flying into a passing scooter's basket — tends to delight students; allow a moment of natural reaction before continuing. Encourage students who read haltingly to follow along with a finger so fluency builds gradually.

periods.activity_title: Comprehension Discussion — Characters, Dialogue and Events

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (p. 15): answer questions 1–3 on Gopi's actions and garden search.
Let us Think A (p. 15): complete dialogue-attribution table (questions a–d).

homework.task_brief: Let us Think A (p. 15): write answers to questions 5 and 6 — who grabbed the ball and why everyone laughed.

time_bands.activity: Quick paired re-read of the playground scene (pp. 13–15). Partners take turns reading one paragraph each to refresh the story in their minds.

Let us Think A — questions 1, 2, and 3 (p. 15): teacher poses each question, students discuss in pairs for a minute, then one pair shares aloud. The teacher uses Gopi's search through grass, bushes, and dry leaves to anchor answers, guiding students to use evidence from the text.

Let us Think A — dialogue-attribution table (p. 15): teacher draws the four-column table on the board (dialogue / said by / said to) and works through one row with the class as a model. Students fill in the remaining three rows in their books, then pairs compare and correct.
Teacher invites one student to read out each completed table row. Any disagreements are resolved by returning briefly to the relevant page of the story.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse who says which line because several characters speak in quick succession at the playground. Encourage them to re-read the relevant dialogue passage rather than guessing from memory. The homework set here asks students to revisit the ball-grabbing episode and the comic ending — both are vividly described in the story and manageable without classroom support.

periods.activity_title: Listen, Draw and Tell — Listening Task and Story-Building

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen A (p. 19): listen to teacher's instructions and draw the scene step by step.

time_bands.activity: Students open their books to the blank space on p. 19. The teacher explains that they will listen carefully to instructions and draw exactly what they hear — no peeking ahead.

Let us Listen A (p. 19): the teacher reads the four-step instructions aloud slowly, repeating each step twice before students begin drawing. Step 1 — big dry leaves with a ball hidden in the middle; Step 2 — twigs; Step 3 — colour leaves yellow and brown, twigs brown; Step 4 — teacher announces 'Now you have found the ball.' Students draw and colour as they listen.
Students hold up their drawings. The teacher invites two or three students to describe what their picture shows in one or two sentences, using the vocabulary from the story — leaves, twigs, ball.

Let us Speak A (p. 19): collaborative story-building chain. The teacher begins with one sentence — 'Once upon a time, a girl found a red ball in her garden.' Each student adds one sentence to continue. The teacher ensures the story moves forward and gently redirects if a sentence contradicts what came before.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening-and-draw task works best when the teacher pauses genuinely between steps — resist reading the next step until most students have begun acting on the current one. The story-chain activity that follows gives every student a low-stakes speaking turn; accept inventive continuations warmly, as the goal is confident oral participation, not a polished story.

periods.activity_title: Think and Speak — Guided Conversation on Honesty and Imagination

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think B (p. 16): guided conversation — what would you do if you found a ball?
Let us Think B (p. 16): imagine the hockey ball's journey after the scooter ride.

time_bands.activity: The teacher recaps the story's key moment — Jay's powerful hit sends the ball into the passing scooter's basket, and the children watch it disappear — to anchor the conversation that follows.

Let us Think B, question 1 (p. 16): guided conversation. The teacher poses 'What would you have done if, like Gopi, you had found a ball that did not belong to you?' Students think silently for one minute, then share in pairs. Four or five students share with the class; the teacher draws out reasoning about honesty and fairness.

Let us Think B, question 2 (p. 16): imagination exercise. 'Where does the hockey ball go after the scooter ride? Who finds it?' Students work in pairs to invent a short continuation. Each pair shares their idea in two or three sentences. The teacher celebrates creative and funny ideas equally.

Let us Think B, question 3 (p. 16): whole-class discussion on helmet safety. The teacher points to the illustration showing the scooterist wearing a helmet and asks why helmets matter and whether the pillion rider should wear one too. Students respond briefly; the teacher affirms correct safety knowledge.

periods.teacher_notes: The honesty question in the first conversation is closely tied to Gopi's character — his decision not to keep the ball is the moral centre of the story. Drawing students back to what Gopi chose helps them ground their opinions in the text rather than speaking in the abstract. The imagination question invites playful invention; treat varied responses as equally valid.

periods.activity_title: Word Meanings and Connectives — Vocabulary and Grammar in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn A (p. 16): match story words — dribble, boast, rustle, grab — to their meanings.
Let us Learn B (p. 17): fill in connectives — since, however, because, when — in Gopi's story.

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes the four words — dribble, boast, rustle, grab — on the board and asks students to guess their meanings from memory of the story. Brief hands-up activity to surface prior understanding.

Let us Learn A (p. 16): matching task. Students work individually to draw lines between each word and its meaning. The teacher then goes through each match aloud, asking a student to use the word in a sentence about the story — for example, using 'grab' in a sentence about Manoj at the playground.

Let us Learn B (p. 17): connectives fill-in. The teacher reads the incomplete story aloud, pausing at each blank. Students choose from since, however, because, when and write their answer. After all four blanks are done, the teacher reads the completed story aloud for students to check their choices make sense.
Paired check: partners swap books and read each other's completed sentences. If they disagree on a blank, they re-read the context together to decide which connective fits.

periods.teacher_notes: Students at this level sometimes confuse 'since' (cause) with 'when' (time) because both can introduce a clause; reading the completed sentence aloud usually reveals which fits naturally. The matching task is grounded in the story itself — 'rustle' and 'dribble' appear in the prose — so students can verify meanings by returning to the text.

periods.activity_title: Adverbs and Long-Short 'oo' — Grammar and Phonics Play

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn C (p. 18): identify and classify adverbs of time and frequency in sentences.
Let us Speak B (p. 20): say words aloud and circle those with a long 'oo' sound.

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes one sentence on the board — 'Gopi immediately got up and ran into the garden' — and asks: 'Which word tells us about the timing of the action?' Brief class response establishes the idea of adverbs before the task begins.

Let us Learn C (p. 18): students work through all seven sentences, encircling the adverb in each and writing 'frequency' or 'time' beside it. The teacher circulates and pauses to discuss sentence (e) — 'Yesterday I ate an ice cream after lunch' — where 'yesterday' as a time adverb can surprise students who expect single-word adverbs only.

Let us Speak B (p. 20): the teacher models the contrast between the short 'oo' in 'book' and the long 'oo' in 'Santoor' / 'scooter'. Students say each of the twelve words aloud and circle those with the long 'oo'. The class reads each word in unison, then individuals call out their verdict — the teacher confirms or corrects.
Quick summary: the teacher asks two students to say one adverb they remember and one long-'oo' word. This closes the word-work orally.

periods.teacher_notes: The adverb classification works best when students read sentences aloud before deciding — they can hear that 'immediately' answers 'when?' rather than 'how many times?' The long/short 'oo' contrast is anchored in the chapter's own title word 'scooter', making the phonics feel purposeful rather than abstract. Students often mis-classify 'shook' and 'foot' as long-'oo' words; brief pair discussion helps them hear the difference.

periods.activity_title: Dialogue Writing — Gopi and Friends After the Scooter

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write A (p. 21): write a conversation between Gopi and friends after the ball is gone.

time_bands.activity: The teacher reminds students of the story's final image — the children watching the scooter disappear with the ball, then bursting into laughter. Class discussion: what might each friend be feeling? Two or three responses are noted on the board to prime the writing.

Modelled writing: the teacher writes Gopi's opening line on the board as an example — a complete, natural-sounding sentence that matches his honest character in the story. The teacher thinks aloud while writing, showing how to give each character a distinct voice.

Let us Write A (p. 21): students write the conversation in their books, giving lines to Gopi, Ramani, Deepak, Manoj, and Jay. The teacher circulates, giving brief formative feedback — prompting students to think about what Deepak (the boastful one) or Ramani (the one who tried to claim the ball) would realistically say.
Two or three students volunteer to read their dialogues aloud to the class. The teacher invites a quick reaction from the audience — which line felt most like the character?

periods.teacher_notes: Encourage students to recall each character's personality from the story when deciding what they say: Deepak boasted about his new football, Ramani tried to claim the ball without proof, and Gopi showed consistent honesty. Students who struggle with getting started can be prompted with 'What would Deepak say about his new football now that this ball is gone too?' Peer sharing at the end values voice, not correctness.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write B (p. 21): form compound words using sun- and foot- and write sentences.
Let us Write C (p. 22): use clues to write nine words containing 'ai' in the middle.

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes 'foot + ball = football' on the board and asks where students encountered 'football' in the chapter (Deepak's boast about his father buying a new one). This links the word-play task to the story's content.

Let us Write B (p. 21): guided writing. The teacher works through 'sun + rise = sunrise' with the class and then students form the remaining five compound words (sunset, sunshine, sunflower, baseball, basketball, volleyball) independently. Students then write one sentence per compound word in their notebooks; the teacher circulates and gives brief feedback on sentence structure.

Let us Write C (p. 22): the teacher reminds students that 'scooter' has 'oo' in the middle — now the chapter gives us words with 'ai'. Students work through clues 2–10 independently, writing each 'ai' word. The teacher invites students to share answers after each set of three clues so any errors are caught early.
Quick class read-aloud of all nine 'ai' words in sequence. Students mark any they got differently and correct silently.

periods.teacher_notes: Let us Write B works well when students say each compound word aloud before writing it — it reinforces that 'basketball' is one word, not two. Let us Write C is a puzzle activity; students who finish quickly can be asked to think of one more 'ai' word not on the list and share it. The transition between the two tasks is smooth because both involve word construction rather than extended writing.

periods.activity_title: Make and Play — Tigers and Goats Board Game

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (p. 23): make the Tigers and Goats board game and play a round.

time_bands.activity: The teacher shows the board pattern diagram on p. 23 and explains the two teams — three tigers (red) and thirteen goats (green) — and the objective of each. Students look at the diagram for one minute before any materials are distributed.

Craft phase: each pair receives a square piece of cardboard and chart paper. Students paste the chart paper, then copy the triangular grid pattern from the diagram on p. 23. The teacher moves around the room, checking that students draw the intersecting lines correctly.

Students collect small pebbles or use torn paper pieces in two colours as tiger and goat tokens. Tokens are placed at starting positions on the board as the teacher explains the movement rules: tigers jump to capture; goats move to surround.
Pairs play one round of Tigers and Goats. The teacher circulates, prompting strategic thinking — 'Can your tiger jump over that goat?' — and ensuring both players understand the winning conditions.
Brief whole-class share-out: who won in each pair, tigers or goats? Students share one moment that surprised them during play.

periods.teacher_notes: The Tigers and Goats game is a traditional strategy game; some students may already know it by another regional name — acknowledge this warmly. The key challenge is drawing the triangular grid accurately, so distribute time generously for the craft phase. If pebbles are unavailable, small torn-paper squares in two colours work equally well as tokens.
materials: Small pebbles or paper tokens in two colours

periods.activity_title: Games Chart, Sports Biography and Hockey Hero Talk

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Explore A (p. 25): prepare a chart of ten games with category columns.
Let us Explore B & C (p. 26): write a mini sports biography and share a hockey player's story.

time_bands.activity: The teacher recalls that hockey is the sport at the centre of the chapter's story and connects it to the wider world of sports. Students are asked to name five sports they know before opening their books.

Let us Explore A (p. 25): the teacher draws the four-column chart on the board — Name of the game / Outdoor or Indoor / Players needed / Equipment needed — and fills in 'Kabaddi' as the model row. Students fill in nine more games of their choice independently, drawing on sports they know or play.

Let us Explore B (p. 26): guided mini biography. The teacher writes the five prompts on the board — name, sport, when and where born, achievement, why inspiring — and students write a short biography of a famous sportsperson they choose. Students who finish quickly are prompted to add one more achievement.

Let us Explore C (p. 26): four or five students share what they know about a famous hockey player in two or three sentences each. The teacher affirms each contribution and adds one factual detail if the class is unfamiliar with the player mentioned.

periods.teacher_notes: The games chart works best when students are encouraged to include sports from their own community or region, not just well-known ones — this often yields the most interesting classroom conversation. For the mini biography, students who cannot recall a sportsperson's details precisely should be encouraged to write what they know and mark gaps with a question mark rather than leaving the whole section blank. The hockey player share-out naturally closes the chapter by returning to the sport that drove the story.

items.item_stem: When Gopi first finds the ball in the garden, what does he decide to do with it?

options.label: A
options.text: He asks around to find out who the ball belongs to.

options.label: B
options.text: He gives it to the nearest shopkeeper.

options.label: C
options.text: He keeps it because no one saw him find it.

options.label: D
options.text: He takes it home and hides it under his bed.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the student may have missed Gopi's honest impulse, which is the story's moral core.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates the student may have confused Gopi's action with a generic lost-property response not supported by the text.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reveals a misreading of Gopi's character; the story explicitly shows he chooses to seek the owner.

items.item_stem: At the playground, Ramani tries to claim the hockey ball even though he cannot prove it is his. What does this tell you about Ramani's character? Give a reason for your answer.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Ramani's attempt to claim the ball without any proof suggests he is dishonest or opportunistic, unlike Gopi who wanted to find the real owner.

items.item_stem: Listen to each instruction your teacher reads and choose the correct answer. — When you finish drawing the scene from Gopi's garden, what colour should the twigs be?

what_each_option_reveals.B: Suggests the student confused the twig colour with the colour of living plants rather than following the instruction.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Indicates the student may have applied the leaf colour (yellow) to the twigs, showing incomplete listening.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals the student did not attend to the colouring instruction at all.
